entities.name: Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Published in 1632 by Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), the Dialogo sopra i Due Massimi Sistemi del Mondo (Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems) is a masterpiece of scientific argumentation and literary art. Written as a conversation between three characters — Salviati (who argues the Copernican heliocentric view), Simplicio (who defends the Ptolemaic geocentric view), and Sagredo (an intelligent layman) — the Dialogue presents a devastating case for heliocentrism based on telescopic observations (the phases of Venus, the moons of Jupiter), the principle of relativity of motion, and a (flawed) tidal theory.

Galileo wrote in Italian rather than Latin, deliberately appealing to the educated public rather than just scholars. Pope Urban VIII, who felt that his own views had been mockingly placed in the mouth of Simplicio (the "simpleton"), was outraged. The book was banned by the Inquisition, and Galileo was tried, forced to recant, and placed under house arrest for the remainder of his life — the most famous conflict between science and religious authority in Western history.

The legendary (apocryphal) phrase "Eppur si muove" ("And yet it moves") captures Galileo's unbroken conviction.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems presented a devastating case for heliocentrism based on telescopic observations and the principle of relativity of motion, challenging geocentric views that had dominated Western Europe for centuries. This led to a significant shift in scientific understanding and paved the way for modern astronomy.
